description: Hi, we are ChocoCherry! We are a pair of early-career professionals looking to build something for fun:)
summary:
Rover Engineer is a free 3D browser game where players design, launch, and operate rovers across progressively harder Moon, Mars, and Titan campaigns. Each campaign pushes players to reconsider engineering trade-offs: heavier equipment adds capability but increases costs, slows travel, consumes more energy, and affects mobility.

In the lunar campaign, players explore the de Gerlache crater rim using NASA LRO elevation data, LROC imagery, changing shadows, and solar-flare events from NASA’s DONKI database. They recharge in sunlight, manage thermal risks, and pursue camera, drilling, and water-ice science objectives. Multiple strategies can succeed, but each mission must generate enough in-game returns to cover its costs.

The game’s increasing difficulty makes trade-offs consequential, encouraging players to experiment, learn from failure, and understand why successful exploration requires balancing scientific ambition with engineering constraints.
details:
What it does and how it works
Rover Engineer is a free 3D browser game about designing rovers for the Moon, Mars and Titan. The player is a new engineer at REL (Rover Exploration Laboratory), a fictional agency. For each mission they pick a chassis, wheels, power, battery, lights, heater and optional instruments, watching mass, size, cost, speed and range on a specification sheet. Mass and size set the launch "ticket" tier, and parts plus ticket must fit the budget. The player then drives the rover in real time.

On the Moon's south pole, one lunar day passes in five minutes: the low Sun sweeps shadows across the land, so the player recharges in sunlight, shelters from solar flares, and avoids freezing in permanent shadow or sinking in soft soil. At Mars's Jezero crater, every night forces a choice between lights on and sleep, and a dust storm dims the panels. On Titan, near where Dragonfly will land, solar power barely works, so the battery must last a long, cold Titan night. A camera or drill earns science milestones, such as finding water ice or photographing a blue Martian sunset. A debrief compares any failure with a real rover that met a similar fate.

Benefits and intended impact
The game teaches that spacecraft subsystems interact: mass alone changes launch price, speed, energy use and sinkage. Each world adds a lesson: mass versus cost on the Moon, a day and night power budget on Mars, a fixed power budget in deep cold on Titan. Players learn by designing, failing and redesigning, like engineers. On the Moon and Mars a mission must earn more than it cost to advance, and several strategies can succeed. On Titan the rover must survive to the end. We want high school learners to understand why real rovers look the way they do, and how NASA data shapes missions from Artemis to Mars 2020 and Dragonfly.

Creativity
The launch ticket turns paying for mass to orbit into a puzzle. On the Moon, players tell time from moving shadows. Each world changes what a good design looks like, every solar flare is a real event, and every failure is compared with a real mission.

Factors we considered
Accuracy versus playability: driving is about four times faster than real, money values are game values, and Titan's terrain is modeled, not measured. A balance check keeps any single build from being best at everything. History facts are optional. The game loads quickly for classroom use, uses no NASA logos, and the agency is fictional.

NASA data
The Moon terrain is the real de Gerlache crater rim from LRO's LOLA laser altimeter, with LOLA illumination and permanent-shadow maps placing the cold zones and hidden ice, and an LROC camera mosaic as the ground texture. Solar flares are real X-class events from NASA's DONKI database, and soil behavior uses Apollo 15 rover results. Mars is Jezero crater from Mars 2020 HiRISE elevation and imagery, with sites placed from Perseverance's real waypoints. Titan's dunes are modeled on Cassini radar measurements, not measured terrain.

Tools
TypeScript, Three.js, Rapier physics, Vite and Vitest for the game; Python with rasterio and NumPy to turn NASA datasets into game files. It runs in any modern desktop browser with no install. Anthropic's Claude, through Claude Code, assisted with research and wrote most of the code under our direction (see the AI disclosure).
